extracted.intended_audience: writers, comedians, students/scholars of humor, and general readers interested in comedic devices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what constitutes a running gag and how it functions in storytelling and comedy, including how they originate, how they generate humor, their forms (verbal/visual), and distinctions from related devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: repeated amusing joke or comical reference
rubrics_metrics.description: A running gag, or running joke, is a literary device that takes the form of an amusing joke or a comical reference and appears repeatedly throughout a work of literature or other form of storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing: 'A running gag, or running joke, is a literary device that takes the form of an amusing joke or a comical reference and appears repeatedly throughout a work of literature or other form of storytelling.' Use repetition across a work to qualify as a running gag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated appearance with variation and audience anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Running gags can begin with an instance of unintentional humor or a one-time joke that provokes a strong response, and is repeated in variations as the joke grows familiar and audiences anticipate reappearances of the gag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing notes the lifecycle: can start accidentally or as one-off, then be repeated in variations; successful running gags leverage audience anticipation of reappearance. Emphasize variation rather than verbatim repeats to keep gag effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underlying content must be a joke (not mere repetition of trivial statements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The humor in a running gag may derive entirely from how often it is repeated, but the underlying statement or situation will always be some form of joke. A trivial statement will not become a running gag simply by being repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse mere repetition with a running gag; ensure the repeated element itself is comedic or becomes comedic through context. Original wording: 'A trivial statement will not become a running gag simply by being repeated.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor source: repetition frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: The humor of a running gag may derive entirely from how often it is repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing, consider using increasing frequency or callbacks to build humor through recognition and expectation. The gag's comedic weight can come from repetition alone if the context supports it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor source: (in)appropriateness and bait-and-switch
rubrics_metrics.description: A running gag may derive its humor from the (in)appropriateness of the situation in which it occurs, or by setting up the audience to expect another occurrence of the joke and then substituting something else (bait and switch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage context incongruity or subverted expectations (bait-and-switch) to refresh the gag and maintain comedic effect. Original phrasing includes explicit mention of 'bait and switch.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins: can begin as unintentional or one-time moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Running gags can begin with an instance of unintentional humor or a one-time joke that provokes a strong response and is then repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to audience reactions; a spontaneous funny moment can be intentionally repeated and developed into a running gag. The page emphasizes that many running gags start this way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form: verbal or visual
rubrics_metrics.description: A running gag can be verbal or visual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers can use dialogue, catchphrases, repeated lines (verbal) or recurring props, visual motifs, or sight gags (visual). The article explicitly states both forms are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct from catchphrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Though related, catchphrases are not considered to be running gags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain distinction: catchphrases are repeated expressions associated with characters, whereas running gags are recurring jokes or references that function across the work. Use this distinction when labeling a repeated element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: applicable across many media and everyday life
rubrics_metrics.description: Running gags are found in everyday life, live theater, live comedy, television shows, video games, films, books, comic strips, and potentially any other situation in which humor is possible and there is enough time for the repetitions to happen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying or evaluating a running gag, consider medium-specific constraints (timing, audience memory, episodic structure). The article lists multiple media to indicate broad applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/semantic function: can convey social values via caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: A running gag may 'convey social values by echoing belligerent speakers with a barrage of caricatured threats.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use running gags not only for laugh value but to satirize or comment on social attitudes; be aware of potential for social critique or reinforcement of stereotypes—this is an indicated function in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example type: self-mocking outrageous propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: For example, a character may present others with a proposition that is so ridiculous or outrageous it is likely to be self-mocking to the point where the original request has little or no chance of actually being carried out and results in a humorous effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a concrete pattern, repeated self-mocking outrageous proposals can function as running gags; the page uses this as an illustrative example (original wording preserved). Consider using such patterns when creating recurring jokes.
